title: Low-latency CPU↔GPU handoff: syscall batching & pinned buffer flow
creator: Lena Zhou
description:
Problem: Production traces for multi-client inference show recurring 200–800µs tail spikes caused by frequent short DMA submissions and host-GPU synchronization points during the prefill→decode transition. These spikes are dominated by per-request syscalls, page-fault handling for newly mapped staging buffers, and small memcpy syscalls queued to the kernel. This increases P95/P99 latency for short sequences and makes our latency SLOs brittle for interactive workloads.

Goal: Reduce host-side overhead in the host→GPU handoff path so that median latency for 1–8 token decode steps improves by >=30% and P95 reduces by >=20% for small-batch workloads, without materially increasing memory overhead or regressing throughput for long-sequence batches.

Proposed approach (summary):
1) Syscall batching: implement a user-space submission queue for small DMA/mapping requests that aggregates operations into a single kernel call per batched group (reduce epoll/ioctl/munmap/mbind churn).
2) Pinned buffer lifecycle: introduce a pinned buffer pool of pre-registered GPU-visible pages (hugepage-backed where supported) that can be reused across requests to avoid page faults and map/unmap latencies during warmups.
3) Doorbell aggregation: coalesce doorbell writes and kernel notifiers for contiguous decode tasks to remove interleaved wakeups from the host threadpool.
4) Lightweight handoff path: add a fast-path that skips heavy scheduling for low-token-count decodes: free-running worker threads perform direct buffer handoff via lock-free ring descriptors to the GPU submission thread.
5) Kernel-aware selection hints: surface light kernel-selection hints from the runtime to drivers (preferred kernel ID for small-batch decode) to prioritize kernels with lower host-sync requirements.

Design trade-offs and notes: We avoid full zero-copy reworks this cycle to keep complexity bounded. The pinned buffer pool will increase resident host memory usage; we'll cap the pool size and use LRU eviction. Syscall batching introduces additional latency for the first op in a batch (a few µs) but overall reduces total wall-clock for groups of short ops. Doorbell aggregation must be careful with backpressure to avoid stalling long-running large-batch workloads.

Measurements and benchmarks: Baseline traces from inference-prod/staging indicate median prefill→decode host-side handoff cost = 360µs, P95 = 1.2ms. Targets: median <= 250µs, P95 <= 960µs for 1–8 token decodes on c6g-highmem-like nodes (or equivalent). We'll run end-to-end against microbench harness (scripts/perf/host_handoff_bench) and synthetic client load with token distributions matching customer traces.

Success criteria:
- Bench harness shows >=30% median improvement and >=20% P95 improvement for short decode steps.
- No regression (>3%) in throughput for long-sequence batches in our throughput suite.
- CI stress for 72 hours shows no increase in OOMs or map-fault spikes.

Rollout plan:
- Feature gated behind runtime flag handoff_opt_v2 and pinned_pool_enabled.
- Canary rollout to 5% of traffic on dedicated clusters, monitor latency dashboards, CPU and page-fault metrics.
- If regression observed, immediate rollback and revert PR.

Implementation notes:
- Kernel submission batching will be implemented in host/submit_queue.cpp as a new SubmissionAggregator class; uses eventfd and a single ioctl to submit grouped ops.
- Pinned pool uses hugetlb-backed mmap where available; fallback to posix_memalign + mlock. Expose pool tuning via config: pinned_pool_size and pinned_hugepage_prealloc.
- Add a lightweight fast-path in host/handoff_fastpath.{h,cc} that uses atomic ring descriptors (borrowed pattern from the user-level NIC queue) to avoid threadpool wakeups for small tasks.
- Drivers/kernels: add a small tag in the submission header to prefer low-host-sync kernels. Runtime will set this based on sequence length heuristics.

Risks and mitigations:
- Increased memory pressure from pinned pages — mitigation: cap pool and enable eviction on pressure, default to small pool size for low-tier customers.
- Edge cases with third-party drivers and hugepages — mitigation: runtime checks and automatic fallback.
- Potential for starvation of the slow-path if fast-path consumes too many GPU slots — mitigation: admission control and fairness counters.
